newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish C.Bank happy with rate gap over Europe.
newsitem.headline: Irish C.Bank happy with rate gap over Europe.

text.p: Ireland's Central Bank said on Thursday that it was happy with the current differential over European interest rates and saw very little room for manoeuvre.
"Current interest rates will be maintained by and large, all things being equal in Europe," a central bank official told a news conference after the release of the quarterly bulletin.
He said interest rates were geared to keep inflation down and current levels were not high enough to restrict economic growth.
The central bank official said a key issue with the bank was to stay on course for monetary union.
"It looks likely we will pass the Maastricht criteria, it is almost a given, as long as we keep inflation at reasonable levels," the official said.

He said Ireland's public finances have been generally well-managed over the past decade. The strong performance of the economy ensured that the Exchequer Borrowing Requirement has been consistently below three percent for several years.

The central bank said this has faciliatated a remarkable reduction in the public debt burden with the debt to GDP ratio expected to amount to 69 percent at the end of 1997, compared to 116 percent at the of 1987.
"This is really a very good performance and brings us very close to the Maastricht guideline of 60 percent," the official said.
He said the bank wanted to maintain a stable 5.5 to 6.0 percent growth rate. "What we do not want is a boom and bust situation," he said.

He said the central bank was concerned about the strong growth in mortgage lending and intended to write to the retail banks, possibly in the next week, to ask them to reflect on certain aspects of mortgage credit.
"It is something we have to check on," he said. "Mortgage lending has been a very rapidly growing part of credit growth."
"If house prices increase it could lead to rising inflation and coming into Maastricht we cannot take that risk," he said.
He said, however, that mortgage lending in Ireland was quite secure and lenders tended to be conservative.
"I don't think they (lenders) are taking unnessessary risks but it is no harm to put a finger on the pulse and take a reading to see if there is a likely cause for a correction."
He said mortgage lending reached double digit growth rates in 1996 and was showing continued strength in 1997.
"The economy is heading into uncharted waters and the central bank wants to make sure panic does not set in if the bubble bursts."
"We could have lean years ahead and we do not want a situation like happened in England of getting into negative equity. That is the fear," he said.
